3. Mr. Nawab Ali learned Advocate-on-Record appearing for the petitioners has argued that the onus of proof was wrongly shifted upon the accused and that the prosecution could not produce any evidence to show that the sale certificate was a forged document. Evidence on which the charge was found to be proved is: P. W. 1 enquired from different offices, such as the Certificate Office, District Record Room, Office of Thana Revenue Officer and the Tahsil Office and found that no Certificate Case as mentioned in the sale certificate was ever filed; P.W. 2 the local Tahsildar; said that no such auction sale was found recorded in the appropriate Register; P.W. 5. a Kanongo said that there was no record in support of the alleged auction-sale; the evidence of three local persons. P.W. 4, 6 and 7 who got lands adjacent to the land in question stated that they did not hear anything about the petitioners purchasing the land in auction. Excepting this sale certificate no document was produced by the petitioners such as rent-receipts, during trial. In this connection, the trial Court observed that the accused persons could not produce anything in support of their purchase in auction. We do not think that onus of proof was thus shifted upon the accused persons. 

 4. Mr. Nawab Ali contends that the sale certificate should have been sent to hand-writing experts for opinion. We do not find any substance therein for when there was no basis for the sale certificate it was useless to send it for expert opinion. Mr. Nawab Ali lastly contends that the petitioners were in possession on the basis of the auction-purchase by paying rent to the Government; but no rent receipt was produced during trial nor any suggestion was made to this effect to the prosecution witnesses. On the contrary, the evidence is that the owner of the land (P.W.3) was forcibly dispossessed by the petitioners. In these circumstances, the High Court Division rightly: refused to interfere with the matter in revision.
